opus-5.5.text:
I think value functions are one of the most underappreciated ideas in the field right now. Think about how reinforcement learning is mostly done today, especially with language models. You have the model try something, it produces a long trajectory, maybe thousands of steps of reasoning, and only at the very end do you get a signal: did it solve the problem or not? If it didn't, you've learned almost nothing from that whole trajectory. That's very inefficient.

A value function lets you short-circuit that. It lets you know, partway through, whether things are going well or badly. If you're playing chess and you lose a piece, you don't need to finish the game to know you made a mistake. You already know. That's what a value function gives you: the ability to get a learning signal long before the final outcome.

What I find interesting is that humans seem to have something like this built in, and it's very robust. You could argue that emotions function partly as a value function. They tell you, in the moment, whether what you're doing is good or bad, whether you should continue. There are fascinating cases of people with damage to the parts of the brain that process emotion. They can still reason and solve puzzles, but they become very bad at making decisions. They'll spend hours deciding which socks to wear. That suggests the value function is doing an enormous amount of work in making us effective agents.

So I think it's very likely that value functions will play a much bigger role going forward. It's not that people haven't thought of them. They're a classic idea. The question is how to make them work well in these new settings, where the tasks are long, open-ended, and hard to evaluate. Once you can learn a good value function, you get much more out of every bit of experience. And I think a lot of the gap between how efficiently humans learn and how efficiently our models learn has to do with exactly this kind of thing.

r001.rationale: The response argues that value functions provide useful intermediate learning signals and are likely to play a larger role. It does not say that anything achievable with a value function can also be achieved without one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think value functions are one of those ideas that are obviously important and yet, for a long time, have been somewhat underutilized in the systems that actually work at scale. Let me try to explain what I mean.

The basic idea is simple. When you are learning from a reward, you can either wait until the very end of an episode and then say, "okay, this whole trajectory was good or bad," or you can try to learn something that tells you, partway through, how well things are going. The second thing is the value function. It is an estimate of the eventual outcome before the outcome has arrived.

Why does that matter? Because the end-of-episode signal is very sparse and very noisy. Imagine you are doing a long chain of reasoning, or a long sequence of actions in an environment, and you only find out at the very end whether it worked. You have to spread that one bit of information across thousands of decisions, and you don't know which of them was the mistake. A good value function lets you localize credit. It lets you notice, at step three hundred, "this is now looking much worse than it did a moment ago," and that is an enormously richer training signal.

Now, the interesting thing is that in the recent wave of reinforcement learning on top of large language models, people have gotten surprisingly far with fairly crude approaches, sometimes with no explicit value function at all, just outcome rewards and lots of samples. And I think the reason that works is that the pretrained model already carries so much prior knowledge that it compensates. The model is, in a sense, already a decent implicit value function for a lot of things. It knows when a proof is going badly.

But I don't think that is where things will stay. If you look at how humans work, we have something like a value function that is extremely good. You feel it when you are solving a problem. You get a sense of "I'm on the right track" or "this is a dead end" long before you reach the answer, and that feeling is what guides your search. It is not perfect, but it is good enough that you rarely have to finish a bad idea to know it was bad. That is what makes human learning so sample efficient compared to what we do with these systems.

So my view is that value functions will become central again, and the real question is where they come from. I don't think the right answer is a separate little network trained on a narrow reward. I think the value function has to be as rich as the policy itself. It has to understand the world, understand the task, and be able to form a judgment about partial progress in the same way the model forms a judgment about anything else. When you have that, you can do something much closer to real search, real deliberation, and the amount of experience you need to learn from goes down dramatically.

And I'd say there is a deeper point hiding here, which is that a good value function is really a form of understanding. To know that a situation is promising, you have to know something true about how it is likely to unfold. So in a way, improving the value function and improving the model's grasp of the world are the same project, just seen from different angles.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can get surprisingly far without an explicit value function, but it does not claim that anything achievable with one is also achievable without one. It instead argues that value functions will become central.

astra-6.text:
I think the value function is a way of answering the question: “How promising is the situation I’m in?” And that’s useful because the consequences of an action may take a long time to become apparent.

Imagine you’re playing chess. You make a move, and perhaps you win forty moves later. The outcome tells you something, but it doesn’t directly tell you which moves were good. A value function lets you estimate how your prospects changed along the way. It gives you a way to learn from intermediate positions, instead of having to wait for the final outcome every time.

It also interacts very naturally with search. You can explore possible continuations, but you can’t explore all of them. So at some point you stop and ask the value function to assess where you’ve arrived. A better value function can make a limited amount of search much more useful.

The difficulty is that the value function is itself learned. It can be wrong, and your policy can find ways to exploit its mistakes. So you need this feedback between what you predict is good and what actually turns out to be good. That’s a big part of what makes reinforcement learning work—and what makes it difficult.

r001.rationale: The response describes value functions as useful for learning from intermediate positions and guiding limited search, but does not say that anything achievable with a value function can also be achieved without one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think value functions are a very natural way of dealing with a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning: you take an action now, but you may only discover much later whether it was useful. A value function tries to predict that future outcome from the situation you’re in today.

Imagine you’re solving a difficult problem. You try an approach, work on it for a while, and eventually get an answer. If the only feedback is whether the final answer is correct, it’s hard to know which intermediate decisions helped. A good value function can give you an earlier signal: this direction looks promising; that direction probably isn’t going anywhere.

But learning that judgment is itself difficult. You need experience that tells you what actually succeeds, and your predictions can be wrong, especially in unfamiliar situations. So I see value functions as a way to make learning and search more efficient. The interesting question is how well they can learn to recognize progress when the solution is still very far away.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes value functions as useful for predicting outcomes and improving learning and search efficiency, but does not say that everything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.
